chunks.text: In 1987, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) succeeded in forging an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels. It is now mandatory for all the manufacturing companies to make CFC-free refrigerators throughout the world. Collect waste material from your homes. This could include all the waste generated during a day, like kitchen waste (spoilt food, vegetable peels, used tea leaves, milk packets and empty cartons), waste paper, empty medicine bottles/strips/bubble packs, old and torn clothes and broken footwear. Bury this material in a pit in the school garden or if there is no space available, you can collect the material in an old bucket/ flower pot and cover with at least 15 cm of soil. Keep this material moist and observe at 15-day intervals.

chunks.source: NCERT Class 10 Science · Ch 13 · Our Environment
chunks.text: Keep this material moist and observe at 15-day intervals. What are the materials that remain unchanged over long periods of time? What are the materials which change their form and structure over time? Of these materials that are changed, which ones change the fastest? Find out from the library, internet or newspaper reports, which chemicals are responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer. Find out if the regulations put in place to control the emission of these chemicals have succeeded in reducing the damage to the ozone layer. Has the size of the hole in the ozone layer changed in recent years? 13.2.2 Managing the Garbage we Produce In our daily activities, we generate a lot of material that are thrown away. What are some of these waste materials?

chunks.source: NCERT Class 10 Science · Ch 13 · Our Environment
chunks.text: What are some of these waste materials? What happens after we throw them away? Let us perform an activity to find answers to these questions. We have seen in the chapter on ‘Life Processes’ that the food we eat is digested by various enzymes in our body. Have you ever wondered why the same enzyme does not break-down everything we eat? Enzymes are specific in their action, specific enzymes are needed for the break-down of a particular substance. That is why we will not get any energy if we try to eat coal! Because of this, many human-made materials like plastics will not be broken down by the action of bacteria or other saprophytes.

chunks.source: NCERT Class 10 Science · Ch 13 · Our Environment
chunks.text: Because of this, many human-made materials like plastics will not be broken down by the action of bacteria or other saprophytes. These materials will be acted upon by physical processes like heat and pressure, but under the ambient conditions found in our environment, these persist for a long time. Substances that are broken down by biological processes are said to be biodegradable. How many of the substances you buried were biodegradable? Substances that are not broken down in this manner are said to be non-biodegradable. These substances may be inert and simply persist in the environment for a long time or may harm the various members of the eco-system.

chunks.source: NCERT Class 10 Science · Ch 13 · Our Environment
chunks.text: Use the library or internet to find out more about biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances. How long are various non-biodegradable substances expected to last in our environment? These days, new types of plastics which are said to be biodegradable are available. Find out more about such materials and whether they do or do not harm the environment. Why are some substances biodegradable and some non-biodegradable? Give any two ways in which biodegradable substances would affect the environment. Give any two ways in which non-biodegradable substances would affect the environment. QUESTIONS Visit any town or city, and we are sure to find heaps of garbage all over the place. Visit any place of tourist interest and we are sure to find the place littered with empty food wrappers.

chunks.source: NCERT Class 10 Science · Ch 13 · Our Environment
chunks.text: Visit any place of tourist interest and we are sure to find the place littered with empty food wrappers. In the earlier classes we have talked about this problem of dealing with the garbage that we generate. Let us now look at the problem a bit more deeply. Our Environment

Disposable cups in trains If you ask your parents, they will probably remember a time when tea in trains was served in plastic glasses which had to be returned to the vendor. The introduction of disposable cups was hailed as a step forward for reasons of hygiene. No one at that time perhaps thought about the impact caused by the disposal of millions of these cups on a daily basis.

chunks.text: The various components of an ecosystem are interdependent. The producers make the energy from sunlight available to the rest of the ecosystem. chunks.question: What is a balanced chemical equation? Why should chemical equations be balanced?
chunks.answer: A balanced chemical equation has an equal number of atoms of each element on both the reactant and product sides (e.g., 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Chemical equations must be balanced to satisfy the Law of Conservation of Mass — mass (atoms) can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

chunks.question: What does one mean by exothermic and endothermic reactions? Give examples.
chunks.answer: Exothermic reactions release heat along with the formation of products — e.g., burning of natural gas: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) + Heat; respiration. Endothermic reactions absorb energy (heat, light or electricity) from the surroundings — e.g., CaCO₃(s) + Heat → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); N₂(g) + O₂(g) + Heat → 2NO(g).

chunks.question: Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction? Explain.
chunks.answer: During digestion, carbohydrates are broken down into glucose. In cells, glucose combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water while releasing energy (ATP + heat): C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(aq) → 6CO₂(aq) + 6H₂O(l) + Energy. Since energy is released, respiration is an exothermic reaction.

chunks.question: Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
chunks.answer: In a combination reaction, two or more substances combine to form a single product (e.g., 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)), whereas in a decomposition reaction, a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances using energy (e.g., 2H₂O(l) --(electricity)--> 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)). Hence they are opposites.

chunks.question: What is the difference between displacement and double displacement reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
chunks.answer: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its salt solution: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange ions in solution to form new compounds (often a precipitate): Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq).

chunks.question: What do you mean by a precipitation reaction? Explain by giving examples.
chunks.answer: Any reaction that produces an insoluble solid (precipitate) which separates out from the solution is called a precipitation reaction. Examples: (1) Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s)↓ (white ppt.) + 2NaCl(aq); (2) AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ (white ppt.) + NaNO₃(aq).

chunks.question: Explain the following in terms of gain or loss of oxygen with two examples each: (a) Oxidation (b) Reduction
chunks.answer: (a) Oxidation is the gain of oxygen by a substance. Examples: (1) 2Cu + O₂ --(Heat)--> 2CuO (copper oxidised to CuO); (2) C + O₂ → CO₂ (carbon oxidised to CO₂). (b) Reduction is the loss of oxygen from a substance. Examples: (1) CuO + H₂ --(Heat)--> Cu + H₂O (CuO reduced to Cu); (2) ZnO + C → Zn + CO (ZnO reduced to Zn).

chunks.question: Why do we apply paint on iron articles?
chunks.answer: Paint forms a protective coating on the surface of iron and cuts off direct contact with air (oxygen) and moisture, thereby preventing rusting (corrosion) of iron.

chunks.question: Oil and fat containing food items are flushed with nitrogen. Why?
chunks.answer: Oils and fats get oxidised in contact with oxygen and become rancid (foul smell and taste). Flushing packets with unreactive nitrogen gas displaces oxygen and acts as an antioxidant, preventing rancidity.

chunks.question: Explain the following terms with one example each: (a) Corrosion (b) Rancidity
chunks.answer: (a) Corrosion: Slow deterioration of metals when attacked by air, moisture or acids around them. Example: Rusting of iron (formation of reddish-brown hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O), or black coating of Ag₂S on silver. (b) Rancidity: Oxidation of fats and oils in food when left exposed to air, causing unpleasant smell and taste. Example: Potato chips or butter turning stale and foul-smelling when kept open.

NCERT answer: (a) Dilute sulphuric acid + Zinc → Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen; H₂SO₄(aq) + Zn(s) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g) (b) Dilute hydrochloric acid + Magnesium → Magnesium chloride + Hydrogen; 2HCl(aq) + Mg(s) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) (c) Dilute sulphuric acid + Aluminium → Aluminium sulphate + Hydrogen; 3H₂SO₄(aq) + 2Al(s) → Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3H₂(g) (d) Dilute hydrochloric acid + Iron → Iron(II) chloride + Hydrogen; 2HCl(aq) + Fe(s) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

chunks.question: Compounds such as alcohols and glucose also contain hydrogen but are not categorised as acids. Describe an Activity to prove it.
chunks.answer: Fix two iron nails on a cork in a beaker and connect them to a 6 V battery through a bulb and switch. Pour dilute HCl — the bulb glows because HCl ionises to give H⁺(aq) ions. Repeat separately with glucose and alcohol solutions — the bulb does NOT glow because glucose and ethanol do not dissociate into H⁺ ions in water, proving they are not acids.

chunks.question: Why does distilled water not conduct electricity, whereas rain water does?
chunks.answer: Distilled water is pure and contains no dissolved ionic salts or free ions to carry charge. Rainwater dissolves atmospheric gases like CO₂ (forming carbonic acid, H₂CO₃) and traces of SO₂/NO₂, producing free H⁺ and anion charge carriers that conduct electricity.

chunks.question: Why do acids not show acidic behaviour in the absence of water?
chunks.answer: Acidic behaviour is due to hydrogen/hydronium ions (H⁺(aq) or H₃O⁺). Separation of H⁺ ions from acid molecules (like HCl) cannot occur without water molecules (HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻); hence dry acids do not show acidic properties.

chunks.question: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is: (a) neutral? (b) strongly alkaline? chunks.answer: (a) Neutral: D (pH 7) (b) Strongly alkaline: C (pH 11) (c) Strongly acidic: B (pH 1) (d) Weakly acidic: A (pH 4) (e) Weakly alkaline: E (pH 9) Increasing order of H⁺ ion concentration (decreasing pH): C (11) < E (9) < D (7) < A (4) < B (1).

chunks.question: Equal lengths of magnesium ribbons are taken in test tubes A and B. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is added to test tube A, while acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is added to test tube B. Amount and concentration taken for both the acids are same. In which test tube will the fizzing occur more vigorously and why?
chunks.answer: Fizzing (evolution of H₂ gas) will occur more vigorously in test tube A (containing HCl). HCl is a strong acid that dissociates completely in water giving a much higher concentration of H⁺ ions than acetic acid (CH₃COOH), which is a weak acid and only partially ionised.

chunks.question: Fresh milk has a pH of 6. How do you think the pH will change as it turns into curd? Explain your answer.
chunks.answer: The pH will decrease below 6 (become more acidic). As milk sets into curd, Lactobacillus bacteria convert lactose sugar into lactic acid, increasing H⁺ ion concentration and lowering pH.

chunks.question: A milkman adds a very small amount of baking soda to fresh milk. (a) Why does he shift the pH of the fresh milk from 6 to slightly alkaline? (b) Why does this milk take a long time to set as curd?
chunks.answer: (a) Making fresh milk slightly alkaline (using mild base NaHCO₃) prevents it from turning sour/spoiling quickly due to lactic acid formation. (b) It takes longer to set as curd because the lactic acid produced initially by bacteria is first used up in neutralising the added baking soda before the pH can drop enough to coagulate milk.

chunks.question: Plaster of Paris should be stored in a moisture-proof container. Explain why?
chunks.answer: Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) readily absorbs moisture from air and hydrates into hard solid gypsum, losing its setting property: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O (Gypsum). Therefore it must be stored in a moisture-proof container.

chunks.question: What is a neutralisation reaction? Give two examples.
chunks.answer: The reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water is called a neutralisation reaction (H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)). Examples: (1) NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l); (2) KOH(aq) + HNO₃(aq) → KNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l).

chunks.question: Give two important uses of washing soda and baking soda.

chunks.question: You are given a hammer, a battery, a bulb, wires and a switch. (a) How could you use them to distinguish between samples of metals and non-metals? (b) Assess the usefulness of these tests in distinguishing between metals and non-metals.
chunks.answer: (a) (i) Hammer test: Strike each sample — metals flatten into thin sheets (malleable) without breaking, whereas non-metals break into pieces (brittle). (ii) Electrical circuit test: Connect each sample between battery, bulb and switch — the bulb glows with metals (good conductors) and generally does not glow with non-metals. (b) These physical tests are quick and useful, though exceptions exist (e.g., graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity; sodium/potassium are soft metals).

chunks.question: What are amphoteric oxides? Give two examples of amphoteric oxides.

chunks.question: Name two metals which will displace hydrogen from dilute acids, and two metals which will not.

chunks.question: In the electrolytic refining of a metal M, what would you take as the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte?
chunks.answer: • Anode: A thick block/rod of impure metal M. • Cathode: A thin strip of pure metal M. • Electrolyte: An acidified aqueous solution of a water-soluble salt of metal M (e.g., acidified CuSO₄ solution for refining copper).

chunks.question: Pratyush took sulphur powder on a spatula and heated it. He collected the gas evolved by inverting a test tube over it. (a) What will be the action of gas on (i) dry litmus paper? (ii) moist litmus paper? (b) Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction taking place.
chunks.answer: (a) Sulphur burns in air to form sulphur dioxide (SO₂) gas: (i) No action on dry litmus paper (no H⁺ ions without water); (ii) Turns moist blue litmus paper red because SO₂ dissolves in water to form sulphurous acid (H₂SO₃). (b) S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g); and SO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₃(aq).

chunks.question: Give reasons: (a) Platinum, gold and silver are used to make jewellery. (b) Sodium, potassium and lithium are stored under oil. (c) Aluminium is a highly reactive metal, yet it is used to make utensils for cooking. (d) Carbonate and sulphide ores are usually converted into oxides during the process of extraction.
chunks.answer: (a) Platinum, gold and silver are very lustrous, highly malleable and ductile, and least reactive — they do not corrode or tarnish easily. (b) Sodium, potassium and lithium are extremely reactive; they react vigorously with oxygen and moisture in air and catch fire, so they are stored under kerosene/paraffin oil. (c) Aluminium forms a tough, thin, non-porous protective layer of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) that prevents further corrosion, and it is a good conductor of heat. (d) It is much easier to obtain a metal by reducing its oxide than directly from its carbonate or sulphide; hence carbonates (by calcination) and sulphides (by roasting) are first converted to oxides.

chunks.question: You must have seen tarnished copper vessels being cleaned with lemon or tamarind juice. Explain why these sour substances are effective in cleaning the vessels.
chunks.answer: Copper reacts slowly with moist CO₂ in air to form a dull green coating of basic copper carbonate (CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂). Lemon and tamarind juice contain acids (citric/tartaric acid) which neutralise and dissolve this basic layer, restoring copper’s shine, while not reacting with copper metal itself.

chunks.question: Differentiate between metal and non-metal on the basis of their chemical properties.
chunks.answer: 1. Metals form basic or amphoteric oxides (e.g., Na₂O, Al₂O₃); non-metals form acidic or neutral oxides (e.g., CO₂, CO). 2. Reactive metals displace H₂ from dilute acids and water; non-metals do not displace H₂ from dilute acids. 3. Metals are electropositive (lose electrons to form cations, acting as reducing agents); non-metals are electronegative (gain/share electrons, acting as oxidising agents).

chunks.question: A man went door to door posing as a goldsmith. He promised to bring back the glitter of old and dull gold ornaments. An unsuspecting lady gave a set of gold bangles to him which he dipped in a particular solution. The bangles sparkled like new but their weight was reduced drastically. The lady was upset but after a futile argument the man beat a hasty retreat. Can you play the detective to find out the nature of the solution he had used?
chunks.answer: He used Aqua Regia — a freshly prepared 3:1 mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) and concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃). Though neither acid alone dissolves gold, aqua regia is highly corrosive and dissolves the outer layer of gold, exposing a shiny inner surface while reducing the bangles’ weight.

chunks.question: Give reasons why copper is used to make hot water tanks and not steel (an alloy of iron).
chunks.answer: Copper does not react with cold water, hot water or steam, and is an excellent conductor of heat. Steel contains iron, which reacts with steam formed from hot water (3Fe + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂) and corrodes over time. Hence copper is preferred.

chunks.question: Explain the nature of the covalent bond using the bond formation in CH₃Cl.
chunks.answer: Carbon (atomic no. 6; 2,4) needs 4 electrons to complete its octet; each H (1) needs 1 electron for its duplet; Cl (2,8,7) needs 1 electron for its octet. Carbon shares three valence electrons with three H atoms (three C–H single covalent bonds) and its fourth valence electron with one Cl atom (one C–Cl single covalent bond), forming covalent CH₃Cl in which every atom attains a noble-gas configuration.

chunks.question: Draw the electron dot structures for: (a) ethanoic acid (b) H₂S (c) propanone (d) F₂
chunks.answer: (a) Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH): Methyl carbon forms 3 single bonds with H and 1 single bond with carboxyl carbon; carboxyl carbon forms a double bond (=O, 2 shared pairs) with one O (having 2 lone pairs) and a single bond with –OH oxygen (having 2 lone pairs and 1 single bond to H). (b) H₂S: Sulphur (6 valence e⁻) shares 1 electron pair with each of two H atoms (H–S–H) and retains 2 lone pairs. (c) Propanone (CH₃COCH₃): Central carbonyl carbon forms single bonds to two –CH₃ groups and a double bond (2 shared pairs) to oxygen (2 lone pairs). (d) F₂: Each F atom (7 valence e⁻) shares 1 electron pair to form F–F, with 3 lone pairs on each F atom.

chunks.question: What is a homologous series? Explain with an example.
chunks.answer: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional group and similar chemical properties in which successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit (14 u molecular mass) and show a regular gradation in physical properties. Example: Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) — CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀; or Alcohols — CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH.

chunks.answer: Physical properties: (1) Ethanol has a pleasant smell and burning taste, whereas ethanoic acid has a pungent vinegar-like smell and sour taste; (2) Melting point of ethanol is 156 K vs 290 K for ethanoic acid (which freezes in winter as glacial acetic acid). Chemical properties: (1) Ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red; ethanol is neutral to litmus. (2) Ethanoic acid reacts with NaHCO₃/Na₂CO₃ giving brisk effervescence of CO₂ gas (CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂↑), whereas ethanol does not react.

chunks.question: Why does micelle formation take place when soap is added to water? Will a micelle be formed in other solvents such as ethanol also?
chunks.answer: A soap molecule has two ends: a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head (–COO⁻Na⁺) and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) long hydrocarbon tail. In water, hydrophobic tails cluster inward away from water while ionic heads point outward into water, forming spherical micelles. Micelles will NOT form in ethanol because the hydrocarbon tail is soluble in ethanol.

chunks.question: Explain the formation of scum when hard water is treated with soap.
chunks.answer: Hard water contains dissolved calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) salts. Soap (sodium/potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids, e.g., C₁₇H₃₅COONa) reacts with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions to form insoluble curdy white precipitates of calcium and magnesium salts of fatty acids called scum: 2C₁₇H₃₅COONa + Ca²⁺ → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca↓ (scum) + 2Na⁺.

chunks.question: What is hydrogenation? What is its industrial application?
chunks.answer: Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen (H₂) to unsaturated hydrocarbons in the presence of catalysts such as nickel (Ni) or palladium (Pd) to form saturated hydrocarbons. Industrial application: Conversion of liquid unsaturated vegetable oils into solid saturated fats (vanaspati ghee) using a nickel catalyst.

chunks.question: Explain the mechanism of the cleaning action of soaps.
chunks.answer: Most dirt is oily in nature and insoluble in water. When soap dissolves in water, its hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails attach to the oily dirt droplet while its hydrophilic ionic heads (–COO⁻Na⁺) face outward into water, forming a micelle trapping the oil at the centre. Mutual ion-ion repulsion keeps micelles dispersed as an emulsion; on agitation and rinsing with water, the trapped oily dirt is washed away.

chunks.question: How are fats digested in our bodies? Where does this process take place?
chunks.answer: Fats are digested in the small intestine. Bile juice from the liver makes the medium alkaline and emulsifies large fat globules into tiny droplets (increasing surface area). Then the enzyme lipase (from pancreatic and intestinal juice) breaks down emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

chunks.answer: Saliva moistens and softens food for easy chewing and swallowing, and contains the enzyme salivary amylase (ptyalin) which breaks down complex starch molecules into simpler sugar (maltose).

chunks.question: What are the necessary conditions for autotrophic nutrition and what are its by-products?
chunks.answer: Necessary conditions for autotrophic nutrition (photosynthesis): carbon dioxide (CO₂), water (H₂O), sunlight and chlorophyll. Its by-products are oxygen (O₂) and water (along with glucose synthesised as food): 6CO₂ + 12H₂O --(Sunlight, Chlorophyll)--> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O.

chunks.question: What are the differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration? Name some organisms that use the anaerobic mode of respiration.
chunks.answer: Aerobic respiration occurs in presence of O₂ (cytoplasm + mitochondria), completely oxidises glucose to CO₂ and H₂O, and yields large energy (38/36 ATP). Anaerobic respiration occurs in absence of O₂ (cytoplasm only), incompletely breaks glucose into ethanol + CO₂ (in yeast) or lactic acid (in muscles), and yields very little energy (2 ATP). Anaerobic organisms: Yeast and certain anaerobic bacteria.

chunks.question: What would be the consequences of a deficiency of haemoglobin in our bodies?
chunks.answer: Haemoglobin is the respiratory pigment in RBCs that transports oxygen from the lungs to all body tissues. Its deficiency (anaemia) reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, leading to lower cellular energy production, fatigue, breathlessness, weakness and pale skin.

chunks.question: Describe double circulation of blood in human beings. Why is it necessary?
chunks.answer: In human double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle: (1) Pulmonary circulation (heart → lungs → heart for oxygenation) and (2) Systemic circulation (heart → body organs → heart to supply O₂). It is necessary to prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, ensuring highly efficient O₂ supply to meet the high energy needs of warm-blooded humans (maintaining constant body temperature).

chunks.question: What are the differences between the transport of materials in xylem and phloem?
chunks.answer: 1. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals; phloem transports prepared food (sucrose), amino acids and hormones. 2. Xylem flow is unidirectional (roots upward to shoots); phloem translocation is bidirectional (upward and downward). 3. Xylem relies mainly on physical forces (root pressure and transpiration pull) without ATP; phloem uses active transport requiring energy (ATP).

chunks.question: Compare the functioning of alveoli in the lungs and nephrons in the kidneys with respect to their structure and functioning.
chunks.answer: Alveoli (functional units of lungs) are thin-walled balloon-like air sacs surrounded by capillaries; they exchange O₂ and CO₂ between inhaled air and blood by diffusion. Nephrons (functional units of kidneys) are tubular units with Bowman’s capsule (containing glomerulus capillaries) and coiled renal tubule; they filter nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid) from blood and selectively reabsorb glucose, amino acids, salts and water to form urine. Both possess huge numbers, vast surface area and dense capillary networks.

chunks.question: What is the function of receptors in our body? Think of situations where receptors do not work properly. What problems are likely to arise?
chunks.answer: Receptors are specialised cells in sense organs that detect environmental stimuli (e.g., gustatory for taste, olfactory for smell, photoreceptors for light, thermoreceptors for heat) and generate nerve impulses. If receptors fail (e.g., blocked nose during a cold, damaged skin thermoreceptors), the body cannot sense spoiled food, gas leaks or hot objects, risking injury or harm.

chunks.question: Draw the structure of a neuron and explain its function.
chunks.answer: A neuron consists of: (1) Dendrites — branched projections receiving information; (2) Cell body (cyton) — containing nucleus and cytoplasm; (3) Axon — long fibre conducting electrical nerve impulses away from the cell body; and (4) Nerve endings — releasing neurotransmitters across the synapse to the next neuron, muscle or gland, enabling rapid signal transmission.

chunks.question: How does phototropism occur in plants?
chunks.answer: Phototropism is directional growth in response to light. When light falls on one side of a plant shoot, the hormone auxin (synthesised at the shoot tip) diffuses towards the shaded side. Higher auxin concentration stimulates cells on the shaded side to elongate more than those on the lit side, causing the shoot to bend towards light.

chunks.question: Which signals will get disrupted in case of a spinal cord injury?
chunks.answer: In a spinal cord injury: (1) Reflex actions mediated by the spinal cord are disrupted; and (2) Both sensory impulses travelling from body receptors to the brain and motor impulses travelling from the brain to muscles/effectors below the injury site are disrupted.

chunks.question: How does chemical coordination occur in plants?
chunks.answer: Plants lack a nervous system and coordinate using chemical messengers called plant hormones (phytohormones), synthesised in one region and diffusing to target sites: Auxins (cell elongation, tropism), Gibberellins (stem growth), Cytokinins (cell division), and Abscisic acid (growth inhibitor, wilting of leaves, stomatal closure).

chunks.question: What is the need for a system of control and coordination in an organism?
chunks.answer: Multicellular organisms have specialised organs and tissues that must work together in an integrated manner, and must respond accurately and promptly to environmental changes (stimuli) for protection, homeostasis, growth and survival — requiring nervous and hormonal control and coordination.

chunks.question: How are involuntary actions and reflex actions different from each other?
chunks.answer: Involuntary actions are automatic ongoing internal processes (like heartbeat, breathing, peristalsis, blood pressure) controlled mainly by the mid-brain and hind-brain (medulla) without an external emergency stimulus. Reflex actions are sudden, rapid, automatic responses to a specific external stimulus (like pulling hand away from a hot object) mediated directly by the spinal cord via a reflex arc.

chunks.question: Compare and contrast nervous and hormonal mechanisms for control and coordination in animals.
chunks.answer: Nervous mechanism sends electrical impulses along neurons (with neurotransmitters at synapses): very fast, highly localised (reaches only innervated cells), and short-lived. Hormonal (endocrine) mechanism secretes hormones into blood: slower, widespread (reaches all target cells throughout the body), and longer-lasting/persistent. Both work together via feedback mechanisms.

chunks.question: What is the difference between the manner in which movement takes place in a sensitive plant and the movement in our legs?
chunks.answer: Movement in a sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) is a nastic response with no nerves or muscles: plant cells change shape by rapidly altering their water content (turgor pressure), causing leaves to fold. Movement in our legs is voluntary, controlled by brain and motor neurons, and occurs when muscle cells shorten/change shape using specialised contractile proteins (actin and myosin).

chunks.question: What are the advantages of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
chunks.answer: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two different individuals, generating greater genetic variation in offspring. These variations increase adaptability to changing environments, improve disease resistance, and ensure long-term survival and evolution of the species, unlike asexual reproduction which produces near-identical clones.

chunks.answer: The testes perform two main functions in human males: (1) Production of male germ-cells (sperms) for reproduction; and (2) Secretion of the male sex hormone testosterone, which regulates sperm formation and brings about secondary sexual characteristics at puberty.

chunks.question: Why does menstruation occur?
chunks.answer: Every month the ovary releases one egg and the uterus prepares a thick, spongy, blood-rich lining (endometrium) to nourish a potential embryo. If the egg is not fertilised, this lining is no longer needed and breaks down slowly, exiting through the vagina as blood and mucous — called menstruation.

chunks.question: Draw a labelled diagram of the longitudinal section of a flower.
chunks.answer: A longitudinal section (L.S.) of a bisexual flower shows four whorls on the receptacle: (1) Sepals (calyx, green protective outer whorl); (2) Petals (corolla, coloured to attract pollinators); (3) Stamens (male part — anther bearing pollen grains + filament); and (4) Pistil/Carpel (female part — sticky stigma at top, tubular style, and swollen basal ovary containing ovules with female germ-cells).

chunks.question: What are the different methods of contraception?
chunks.answer: 1. Mechanical barrier methods: Condoms or cervical caps prevent sperm from reaching the egg (condoms also protect against STDs). 2. Chemical/hormonal methods: Oral contraceptive pills alter hormonal balance to prevent ovulation. 3. Intrauterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCDs): Copper-T or loop placed in the uterus prevents pregnancy. 4. Surgical (permanent) methods: Vasectomy (blocking vas deferens in males) and Tubectomy (blocking fallopian tubes in females).

chunks.question: How are the modes for reproduction different in unicellular and multicellular organisms?
chunks.answer: Unicellular organisms consist of a single cell and reproduce mainly by simple asexual methods such as binary fission (Amoeba), multiple fission (Plasmodium) or budding (Yeast). Multicellular organisms have differentiated tissues and specialised reproductive organs, so cell-by-cell division cannot work; they reproduce via complex methods such as spore formation, vegetative propagation or sexual reproduction involving gametes.

How are the modes for reproduction different in unicellular and multicellular organisms?
NCERT answer: Unicellular organisms consist of a single cell and reproduce mainly by simple asexual methods such as binary fission (Amoeba), multiple fission (Plasmodium) or budding (Yeast). Multicellular organisms have differentiated tissues and specialised reproductive organs, so cell-by-cell division cannot work; they reproduce via complex methods such as spore formation, vegetative propagation or sexual reproduction involving gametes.

chunks.question: How does reproduction help in providing stability to populations of species?
chunks.answer: Reproduction creates new individuals carrying the species’ DNA body design to replace organisms lost to ageing, predation and death, maintaining population numbers. Additionally, DNA variations generated during reproduction allow some individuals to survive drastic environmental changes, preventing extinction.

chunks.question: How do Mendel's experiments show that traits may be dominant or recessive?
chunks.answer: Mendel crossed pure tall (TT) pea plants with pure dwarf (tt) plants. All F₁ progeny (Tt) were tall — no dwarf or medium plants appeared, showing tallness (T) is dominant. On self-pollinating F₁ plants, F₂ progeny produced tall and dwarf plants in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt), proving the dwarf trait (t) was recessive (present in F₁ but expressed only when homozygous tt).

chunks.question: How do Mendel's experiments show that traits are inherited independently?
chunks.answer: In a dihybrid cross between pea plants with round-yellow seeds (RRYY) and wrinkled-green seeds (rryy), all F₁ seeds were round-yellow (RrYy). On selfing F₁, the F₂ generation showed a 9:3:3:1 ratio — round-yellow (9), round-green (3), wrinkled-yellow (3), wrinkled-green (1). The appearance of two new non-parental combinations (round-green and wrinkled-yellow) proves seed shape and seed colour assort independently.

chunks.question: A man with blood group A marries a woman with blood group O and their daughter has blood group O. Is this information enough to tell you which of the traits - blood group A or O - is dominant? Why or why not?
chunks.answer: No, this information alone is not sufficient. Case 1: If A is dominant, a heterozygous father (Iᴬi) and mother (ii) can produce a daughter with blood group O (ii). Case 2: If O were dominant, a father (aa) and heterozygous mother (Oo) could also produce a daughter with group O (Oo). Since both hypotheses explain the child’s blood group, dominance cannot be deduced from this single cross alone.

chunks.question: How is the sex of the child determined in human beings?
chunks.answer: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 autosome pairs and 1 pair of sex chromosomes — XX in females and XY in males. All eggs carry an X chromosome, while half the sperms carry X and half carry Y. If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg, the zygote is XX (girl); if a Y-bearing sperm fertilises the egg, the zygote is XY (boy). Thus sex is determined by the chromosome inherited from the father (50:50 chance).

chunks.chapterTitle: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
chunks.question: Why do stars twinkle?
chunks.answer: Stars are very distant point-sized sources of light. Starlight undergoes continuous atmospheric refraction through layers of air of gradually increasing refractive index. Because the atmosphere’s physical conditions (temperature, density) constantly fluctuate, the apparent position of the star and the amount of starlight entering the eye flicker continuously, making stars twinkle.

chunks.chapterTitle: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
chunks.question: Explain why the planets do not twinkle.
chunks.answer: Planets are much closer to Earth and appear as extended sources — a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light. Random variations in light entering the eye from individual point sources cancel out and average to zero, so their apparent brightness stays steady and planets do not twinkle.

chunks.answer: (i) For 9 Ω: Connect two 6 Ω resistors in parallel and connect the third 6 Ω resistor in series with this parallel pair. R_p = (6 × 6)/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω; then R_eq = 6 Ω + 3 Ω = 9 Ω. (ii) For 4 Ω: Connect two 6 Ω resistors in series (R_s = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω) and connect the third 6 Ω resistor in parallel across them. 1/R_eq = 1/12 + 1/6 = 3/12 = 1/4 ⇒ R_eq = 4 Ω.

chunks.question: Compare the power used in the 2 Ω resistor in each of the following circuits: (i) a 6 V battery in series with 1 Ω and 2 Ω resistors, and (ii) a 4 V battery in parallel with 12 Ω and 2 Ω resistors.
chunks.answer: (i) Series circuit (6 V with 1 Ω and 2 Ω): R_total = 1 + 2 = 3 Ω; current I = V/R = 6/3 = 2 A. Power in 2 Ω resistor = I²R = (2)² × 2 = 8 W. (ii) Parallel circuit (4 V across 12 Ω and 2 Ω): Potential difference across 2 Ω resistor is V = 4 V. Power in 2 Ω resistor = V²/R = (4)²/2 = 16/2 = 8 W. Conclusion: Both circuits consume the same power (8 W) in the 2 Ω resistor.

chunks.question: Explain the following: (a) Why is the tungsten used almost exclusively for filament of electric lamps? (b) Why are the conductors of electric heating devices, such as bread-toasters and electric irons, made of an alloy rather than a pure metal? (c) Why is the series arrangement not used for domestic circuits? (d) How does the resistance of a wire vary with its area of cross-section? (e) Why are copper and aluminium wires usually employed for electricity transmission?
chunks.answer: (a) Tungsten has an extremely high melting point (3380 °C) and high resistivity, so it glows white-hot without melting. (b) Alloys have higher resistivity than pure constituent metals and do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures. (c) In series, if one appliance fails the entire circuit breaks, appliances cannot be switched independently, each gets reduced voltage, and high- and low-power devices cannot draw their required currents. (d) Resistance is inversely proportional to area of cross-section (R ∝ 1/A): thicker wires have lower resistance. (e) Copper and aluminium have very low electrical resistivity (minimising I²R heat loss) and are ductile and economical.

chunks.question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
chunks.answer: An electric short circuit occurs when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact (due to damaged/worn insulation or an appliance fault). Circuit resistance drops almost to zero, causing current to rise abruptly and dangerously.

chunks.question: What is the function of an earth wire? Why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
chunks.answer: The earth wire (green insulation, connected to a metal plate deep in the ground) provides a low-resistance conducting path for leakage current. Earthing metallic-bodied appliances ensures that if live wire touches the metal casing, its potential remains equal to earth potential and leakage current flows safely to ground, protecting the user from severe electric shock.

chunks.question: What will happen if we kill all the organisms in one trophic level?
chunks.answer: Killing all organisms in one trophic level disrupts the food chain: organisms in the next higher trophic level will starve and decline due to lack of food, while organisms in the trophic level just below will multiply unchecked, creating severe ecological imbalance.

chunks.question: Will the impact of removing all the organisms in a trophic level be different for different trophic levels? Can the organisms of any trophic level be removed without causing any damage to the ecosystem?
chunks.answer: Yes, the impact varies by trophic level — e.g., removing producers collapses the entire ecosystem, while removing top carnivores causes herbivore overpopulation and overgrazing of vegetation. No, organisms of any trophic level cannot be completely removed without damaging the ecosystem because all trophic levels are interdependent.

chunks.question: What is biological magnification? Will the levels of this magnification be different at different levels of the ecosystem?
chunks.answer: Biological magnification (biomagnification) is the progressive increase in concentration of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals (such as DDT, pesticides, heavy metals) at successive trophic levels of a food chain. Yes, levels increase up the food chain and are highest at the top trophic level (e.g., human beings and predatory birds).

chunks.question: If all the waste we generate is biodegradable, will this have no impact on the environment?
chunks.answer: No — excessive biodegradable waste still impacts the environment if generated faster than decomposers can break it down: heaps produce foul odours and toxic/greenhouse gases (methane, CO₂), pollute water bodies (eutrophication/oxygen depletion), and act as breeding grounds for flies, mosquitoes and disease-causing microbes.

chunks.question: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? What steps are being taken to limit this damage?
chunks.answer: The stratospheric ozone layer (O₃) shields life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which causes skin cancer, cataracts, immune damage and harm to crops/plankton. Steps taken: Under UNEP’s 1987 Montreal Protocol, nations froze CFC production at 1986 levels and mandated CFC-free refrigerators, ACs and aerosols.
